{{Short description|Generalization of Rice's theorem}}
In [[recursion theory|computability theory]], the '''Rice–Shapiro theorem''' is a generalization of [[Rice's theorem]], named after [[Henry Gordon Rice]] and [[Norman Shapiro]]. It states that when a [[computably enumerable set|semi-decidable]] property of [[general recursive function|partial computable functions]] is true on a certain [[partial function]], one can extract a ''finite'' subfunction such that the property is still true.

The informal idea of the theorem is that the "only general way" to obtain information on the behavior of a program is to run the program, and because a computation is finite, one can only try the program on a finite number of inputs.

A closely related theorem is the '''Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin theorem''' (or '''KLST theorem'''), which was obtained independently by [[Georg Kreisel]], Daniel Lacombe and [[Joseph R. Shoenfield]]{{r|kls}}, and by [[Grigori Tseitin]]{{r|tseitin}}.

==Formal statement==

'''Rice-Shapiro theorem.'''{{r|rogers|p=482}}{{r|cutland}}{{r|odifreddi}} Let <math>P</math> be a set of [[general recursive function|partial computable functions]] such that the [[index set (computability)|index set]] of <math>P</math> (i.e., the set of indices <math>e</math> such that <math>\phi_e \in P</math>, for some fixed [[admissible numbering]] <math>\phi</math>) is [[computably enumerable set|semi-decidable]]. Then for any partial computable function <math>f</math>, it holds that <math>P</math> contains <math>f</math> if and only if <math>P</math> contains a ''finite'' subfunction of <math>f</math> (i.e., a partial function defined in finitely many points, which takes the same values as <math>f</math> on those points).

'''Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin theorem.'''{{r|rogers|p=362}}{{r|kls}}{{r|tseitin}}{{r|moschovakis}}{{r|royer}}{{r|longley-normann|p=440}} Let <math>P</math> be a set of [[general recursive function|total computable functions]] such that the index set of <math>P</math> is [[computable set|decidable]] with a [[promise problem|promise]] that the input is the index of a total computable function (i.e., there is a partial computable function <math>D</math> which, given an index <math>e</math> such that <math>\phi_e</math> is total, returns 1 if <math>\phi_e \in P</math> and 0 otherwise; <math>D(e)</math> need not be defined if <math>\phi_e</math> is not total). We say that two total functions <math>f</math>, <math>g</math> "agree until <math>n</math>" if <math>f(k) = g(k)</math> holds for all <math>k \leq n</math>. Then for any total computable function <math>f</math>, there exists <math>n</math> such that for all total computable function <math>g</math> which agrees with <math>f</math> until <math>n</math>, we have <math>f \in P \iff g \in P</math>.

==Examples==

By the Rice-Shapiro theorem, it is neither semi-decidable nor co-semi-decidable whether a given program:

* Terminates on all inputs ([[halting problem # halting on all inputs|universal halting problem]]);
* Terminates on finitely many inputs;
* Is equivalent to a fixed other program.

By the Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin theorem, it is undecidable whether a given program ''which is assumed to always terminate'':

* Always returns an [[Parity (mathematics)|even number]];
* Is equivalent to a fixed other program that always terminates;
* Always returns the same value.

==Discussion==

The two theorems are closely related, and also relate to [[Rice's theorem]]. Specifically:
* Rice's theorem applies to ''decidable'' sets of ''partial computable'' functions, concluding that they must be trivial.
* The Rice-Shapiro theorem applies to ''semi-decidable'' sets of ''partial computable'' functions, concluding that they can only recognize elements based on a finite number of values.
* The Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin theorem applies to ''decidable'' sets of ''total computable'' functions, with a conclusion similar to the Rice-Shapiro theorem.

It is natural to wonder what can be said about ''semi-decidable'' sets of ''total computable'' functions. Perhaps surprisingly, these need ''not'' verify the conclusion of the Rice-Shapiro and Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin theorems. The following counterexample is due to [[Richard M. Friedberg]].{{r|friedberg}}{{r|longley-normann|p=444}}

Let <math>Q</math> be the set of total computable functions <math>f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}</math> such that <math>f</math> is not the constant zero function and, defining <math>n</math> to be the maximum index such that <math>f(n)</math> is zero, there exists a program of code <math>e \leq n</math> such that <math>\phi_e(i)</math> is defined and equal to <math>f(i)</math> for each <math>i \leq n+1</math>. Let <math>P</math> be the set <math>Q</math> with the constant zero function added.

On the one hand, <math>P</math> contains the constant zero function by definition, yet there is no <math>n</math> such that if a total computable <math>g</math> agrees with the constant zero function until <math>n</math> then <math>g \in P</math>. Indeed, given <math>n</math>, we can define a total function <math>g</math> by setting <math>g(n+1)</math> to some value larger than every <math>\phi_e(n+1)</math> for <math>e \leq n+1</math> such that <math>\phi_e(n+1)</math> is defined, and <math>g(n') = 0</math> for <math>n' \neq n+1</math>. The function <math>g</math> is zero except on the value <math>n+1</math>, thus computable, it agrees with the zero function up to <math>n</math>, but it does not belong to <math>P</math> by construction.

On the other hand, given a program <math>e</math> and a promise that <math>\phi_e</math> is total, it is possible to semi-decide whether <math>\phi_e \in P</math> by dovetailing, running one task to semi-decide <math>\phi_e \in Q</math>, which can clearly be done, and another task to semi-decide whether <math>\phi_e(k) = 0</math> for all <math>k \leq e</math>. This is correct because the zero function is detected by the second task, and conversely, if the second task returns true, then either <math>\phi_e</math> is zero, or <math>\phi_e</math> is only zero up to an index <math>n</math>, which must satisfy <math>e \leq n</math>, which by definition of <math>Q</math> implies that <math>\phi_e \in Q</math>.

==Proof of the Rice-Shapiro theorem==

Let <math>P</math> be a set of partial computable functions with semi-decidable index set. We prove the two implications separately.

===Upward closedness===

We first prove that if <math>f</math> is a finite subfunction of <math>g</math> and <math>f \in P</math> then <math>g \in P</math>. The hypothesis that <math>f</math> is finite is in fact of no use.

The proof uses a [[Diagonal argument (proof technique)|diagonal argument]] typical of theorems in computability. We build a program <math>p</math> as follows. This program takes an input <math>x</math>. Using a standard [[dovetailing (computer science)|dovetailing]] technique, <math>p</math> runs two tasks in parallel.
* The first task executes a [[semi-algorithm]] that semi-decides <math>P</math> on <math>p</math> itself (<math>p</math> can get access to its own source code by [[Kleene's recursion theorem]]). If this eventually returns true, then this first task continues by executing a semi-algorithm that semi-computes <math>g</math> on <math>x</math> (the input to <math>p</math>), and if that terminates, then the task makes <math>p</math> as a whole return <math>g(x)</math>.
* The second task runs a semi-algorithm that semi-computes <math>f</math> on <math>x</math>. If this returns true, then the task makes <math>p</math> as a whole return <math>f(x)</math>.

If <math>\phi_p \notin P</math>, the first task can never finish, therefore the result of <math>p</math> is entirely determined by the second task, thus <math>\phi_p</math> is simply <math>f</math>, a contradiction. This shows that <math>\phi_p \in P</math>.

Thus, both tasks are relevant; however, because <math>f</math> is a subfunction of <math>g</math> and the second task returns <math>f(x) = g(x)</math> when <math>f(x)</math> is defined, while the first task returns <math>g(x)</math> when defined, the program in fact computes <math>g</math>, i.e., <math>\phi_p = g</math>, and therefore <math>g \in P</math>.

===Extracting a finite subfunction===

Conversely, we prove that if <math>P</math> contains a partial computable function <math>f</math>, then it contains a finite subfunction of <math>f</math>. Let us fix <math>f \in P</math>. We build a program <math>p</math> which takes input <math>x</math> and runs the following steps:
* Run <math>x</math> computation steps of a semi-algorithm that semi-decides <math>P</math>, with <math>p</math> itself as input. If this semi-algorithm terminates and returns true, then loop indefinitely.
* Otherwise, semi-compute <math>f</math> on <math>x</math>, and if this terminates, return the result <math>f(x)</math>.

Suppose that <math>\phi_p \notin P</math>. This implies that the semi-algorithm for semi-deciding <math>P</math> used in the first step never returns true. Then, <math>p</math> computes <math>f</math>, and this contradicts the assumption <math>f \in P</math>. Thus, we must have <math>\phi_p \in P</math>, and the algorithm for semi-deciding <math>P</math> returns true on <math>p</math> after a certain number of steps <math>n</math>. The partial function <math>\phi_p</math> can only be defined on inputs <math>x</math> such that <math>x \leq n</math>, and it returns <math>f(x)</math> on such inputs, so it is a finite subfunction of <math>f</math> that belongs to <math>P</math>.

==Proof of the Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin theorem==

===Preliminaries===

A total function <math>h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}</math> is said to be ultimately zero if it always takes the value zero except for a finite number of points, i.e., there exists <math>N</math> such that <math>h(n) = 0</math> for all <math>n \geq N</math>. Note that such a function is always computable (it can be computed by simply checking if the input is in a certain predefined list, and otherwise returning zero).

We fix <math>U</math> a computable enumeration of all total functions which are ultimately zero, that is, <math>U</math> is such that:
* For all <math>k</math>, the function <math>\phi_{U(k)}</math> is ultimately zero;
* For all total function <math>h</math> which is ultimately zero, there exists <math>k</math> such that <math>\phi_{U(k)} = h</math>;
* The function <math>U</math> is itself total computable.

We can build <math>U</math> by standard techniques (e.g., for increasing <math>N</math>, enumerate ultimately zero functions which are bounded by <math>N</math> and zero on inputs larger than <math>N</math>).

===Approximating by ultimately zero functions===

Let <math>P</math> be as in the statement of the theorem: a set of total computable functions such that there is an algorithm which, given an index <math>e</math> and a [[promise problem|promise]] that <math>\phi_e</math> is total, decides whether <math>\phi_e \in P</math>. 

We first prove a lemma: For all total computable function <math>f</math>, and for all integer <math>N</math>, there exists an ultimately zero function <math>h</math> such that <math>h</math> agrees with <math>f</math> until <math>N</math>, and <math>f \in P \iff h \in P</math>.

To prove this lemma, fix a total computable function <math>f</math> and an integer <math>N</math>, and let <math>B</math> be the boolean <math>f \in P</math>. Build a program <math>p</math> which takes input <math>x</math> and takes these steps:
* If <math>x \leq N</math> then return <math>f(x)</math>;
* Otherwise, run <math>x</math> computation steps of the algorithm that decides <math>P</math> on <math>p</math>, and if this returns <math>B</math>, then return zero;
* Otherwise, return <math>f(x)</math>.

Clearly, <math>p</math> always terminates, i.e., <math>\phi_p</math> is total. Therefore, the promise to <math>P</math> run on <math>p</math> is fulfilled.

Suppose for contradiction that one of <math>f</math> and <math>\phi_p</math> belongs to <math>P</math> and the other does not, i.e., <math>(\phi_p \in P) \neq B</math>. Then we see that <math>p</math> computes <math>f</math>, since <math>P</math> does not return <math>B</math> on <math>p</math> no matter the amount of steps. Thus, we have <math>f = \phi_p</math>, contradicting the fact that one of <math>f</math> and <math>\phi_p</math> belongs to <math>P</math> and the other does not. This argument proves that <math>f \in P \iff \phi_p \in P</math>. Then, the second step makes <math>p</math> return zero for sufficiently large <math>x</math>, thus <math>\phi_p</math> is ultimately zero; and by construction (due to the first step), <math>\phi_p</math> agrees with <math>f</math> until <math>N</math>. Therefore, we can take <math>h = \phi_p</math> and the lemma is proved.

===Main proof===

With the previous lemma, we can now prove the Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin theorem. Again, fix <math>P</math> as in the theorem statement, let <math>f</math> be a total computable function and let <math>B</math> be the boolean "<math>f \in P</math>". Build the program <math>p</math> which takes input <math>x</math> and runs these steps:
* Run <math>x</math> computation steps of the algorithm that decides <math>P</math> on <math>p</math>.
* If this returns <math>B</math> in a certain number of steps <math>n</math> (which is at most <math>x</math>), then search in parallel for <math>k</math> such that <math>U(k)</math> agrees with <math>f</math> until <math>n</math> and <math>(U(k) \in P) \neq B</math>. As soon as such a <math>k</math> is found, return <math>U(k)(x)</math>.
* Otherwise (if <math>P</math> did not return <math>B</math> on <math>p</math> in <math>x</math> steps), return <math>f(x)</math>.

We first prove that <math>P</math> returns <math>B</math> on <math>p</math>. Suppose by contradiction that this is not the case (<math>P</math> returns <math>\lnot B</math>, or <math>P</math> does not terminate). Then <math>p</math> actually computes <math>f</math>. In particular, <math>\phi_p</math> is total, so the promise to <math>P</math> when run on <math>p</math> is fulfilled, and <math>P</math> returns the boolean <math>\phi_p \in P</math>, which is <math>f \in P</math>, i.e., <math>B</math>, contradicting the assumption.

Let <math>n</math> be the number of steps that <math>P</math> takes to return <math>B</math> on <math>p</math>. We claim that <math>n</math> satisfies the conclusion of the theorem: for all total computable function <math>g</math> which agrees with <math>f</math> until <math>n</math>, it holds that <math>f \in P \iff g \in P</math>. Assume for contradiction that there exists <math>g</math> total computable which agrees with <math>f</math> until <math>n</math> and such that <math>(g \in P) \neq B</math>.

Applying the lemma again, there exists <math>k</math> such that <math>U(k)</math> agrees with <math>g</math> until <math>n</math> and <math>g \in P \iff U(k) \in P</math>. Since both <math>U(k)</math> and <math>f</math> agree with <math>g</math> until <math>n</math>, <math>U(k)</math> also agrees with <math>f</math> until <math>n</math>, and since <math>(g \in P) \neq B</math> and <math>g \in P \iff U(k) \in P</math>, we have <math>(U(k) \in P) \neq B</math>.  Therefore, <math>U(k)</math> satisfies the conditions of the parallel search step in the program <math>p</math>, namely: <math>U(k)</math> agrees with <math>f</math> until <math>n</math> and <math>(U(k) \in P) \neq B</math>. This proves that the search in the second step always terminates. We fix <math>k</math> to be the value that it finds.

We observe that <math>\phi_p = U(k)</math>. Indeed, either the second step of <math>p</math> returns <math>U(k)(x)</math>, or the third step returns <math>f(x)</math>, but the latter case only happens for <math>x \leq n</math>, and we know that <math>U(k)</math> agrees with <math>f</math> until <math>n</math>.

In particular, <math>\phi_p = U(k)</math> is total. This makes the promise to <math>P</math> run on <math>p</math> fulfilled, therefore <math>P</math> returns <math>\phi_p \in P</math> on <math>p</math>.

We have found a contradiction: one the one hand, the boolean <math>\phi_p \in P</math> is the return value of <math>P</math> on <math>p</math>, which is <math>B</math>, and on the other hand, we have <math>\phi_p = U(k)</math>, and we know that <math>(U(k) \in P) \neq B</math>.

== Topological view ==

The set of total computable functions can be viewed as a subspace of the [[Baire space (set theory)|Baire space]] <math>\mathcal{T} \subseteq \N^\N</math>. The Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin theorem states that if a function <math>F : \mathcal{T} \to 2</math> (where the set of booleans <math>2</math> has the [[discrete topology]]) is computable (from a program computing <math>f \in \mathcal{T}</math>, we can compute <math>F(f)</math>), then <math>F</math> must be continuous.

The above proof of the Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin gives a strengthening of the theorem: from programs computing <math>F</math> and <math>f</math>, one can compute <math>n</math> such that <math>F</math> is constant on functions agreeing with <math>f</math> until <math>n</math>. This strengthened version has a natural interpretation from the point of view of [[realizability]]: inside the internal logic of the [[effective topos]], it holds that every function <math>\N^\N \to 2</math> is continuous.{{r|van-oosten-klst-brouwer}}

For the Rice–Shapiro theorem, one views the set of partial computable functions as a subspace of the space <math>\mathcal{P}</math> of all partial functions from <math>\N</math> to <math>\N</math> topologized in the following way: for each finite partial function <math>f</math>, the set of partial functions extending <math>f</math> is declared to be a [[Base (topology)|basic open set]]. The theorem states that if a subset <math>P \subseteq \mathcal{P}</math> is semi-decidable (from a program computing <math>f \in \mathcal{P}</math>, we can semi-decide whether <math>f \in P</math>), then it must be open.
